title: Sincere repentance
hookLine: turn to Allah in sincere repentance (66:8)

cards: There's the fake apology. "I'm sorry you feel that way." "Mistakes were made."
The sorry that's mostly about getting the conversation over with. And there's the rarer kind, where you can hear that the person has actually stopped, looked at what they did, and turned around.
Surah sixty-six, at-Tahrim, has a name for that second kind. It asks the believers for a repentance that is, in its word, nasuh.

teach.b: Verse eight, in Pickthall: "O ye who believe! Turn unto Allah in sincere repentance!" The Arabic is tawbatan nasuha. Tawbah, repentance, comes from a root that means to return.
It's not mainly about feeling bad. It's about turning around and walking home.
And one of the names of Allah comes from the same root: at-Tawwab, the One who turns, again and again, toward the one who turns back. Both sides are moving. Nasuh is the hard part.
It shares a root with nasihah, sincere advice, the kind a true friend gives. A nasuh repentance has nothing hidden in it, no deal on the side, no plan to do it again on Friday.
Scholars such as Imam an-Nawawi set out what that looks like.
You stop the wrong thing. You regret it. You resolve not to return to it.

And if it hurt another person, there's a fourth step: make it right with them, return what was taken, ask their pardon. A hadith in Ibn Majah puts the heart of it in a few words: regret is repentance.
And the verse comes with hope, not a scolding: perhaps your Lord will remit your bad deeds. Not perhaps you'll earn it. Perhaps He will.

teach.h: SINCERE ISN'T THE SAME AS PERFECT.
teach.b: One more thing: sincere doesn't mean perfect. In the scholarly tradition, someone who truly repents and later slips hasn't made the first repentance fake. They turn back again.
The door doesn't lock after the first use.

how: Muslims repent (tawbah) by stopping a wrong, regretting it and resolving not to return to it, and, when another person was harmed, by making amends; astaghfirullah, I seek Allah's forgiveness, is a familiar phrase of daily speech.

o: a turning back to God with nothing hidden
feeling guilty until the guilt fades away
a formal confession made before a judge

p: the One who turns again and again
make it right with the one harmed

s: its root means to return: it's turning around and coming back.
if you slip after repenting, the first repentance was fake
in the scholarly tradition, sincere isn't perfect; you turn back again.
at-Tawwab shares a root with tawbah
the One who turns toward people as they turn back.

games.q: you wronged a friend and you're truly sorry before Allah. by the scholars' steps, is regret enough?
o: no, you also make it right with your friend.
games.why: when a wrong touched another person, scholars like an-Nawawi add a fourth step: repair it with them, or ask their pardon.

practice: Let one thing come up, not your whole life, one thing, maybe small: a sharp word, a corner cut. Walk it quietly through the four steps: can I stop, do I regret it, will I not go back, is there someone I owe a repair?
If you pray, this is a moment for astaghfirullah, I seek Allah's forgiveness; if you don't, simply turn toward the better thing.

wordCard.voice: Sincere repentance. Tawbatan nasuha, a turning back with nothing hidden in it: stop, regret, resolve, and repair what you broke. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a sincere repentance (66:8). tawbah, a turning back; nasuh, pure of any hidden motive.

carryVoice: Your line: turn back sincerely. Sincere, not perfect; you can always turn again. Day six hundred thirty-four, done.

sources.q: O ye who believe! Turn unto Allah in sincere repentance!
